channel.title: The Dead Web Gazette
channel.description: A periodical of digital archaeology: illustrated, sourced memorials for things the internet used to have.

item.title: Winamp
item.description: The skinnable player that owned the MP3 era -- it really whips the llama.

item.title: Vine
item.description: Six seconds, looping forever -- the app that taught a generation comedy in one breath.

item.title: StumbleUpon
item.description: A button that took you somewhere you never would have gone, and the web that stopped pressing it.

item.title: Something Awful
item.description: The pay-to-post comedy forum that incubated the internet's sense of humor, and outlived its founder.

item.title: Posterous
item.description: The blog you wrote by sending an email, acquired by the company that then deleted the emails.

item.title: Pets.com
item.description: A sock puppet, a Super Bowl ad, and nine months from IPO to liquidation.

item.title: Newgrounds
item.description: The Flash portal where a generation of animators learned to ship, still open after the Flash went out.

item.title: Napster
item.description: Eighteen months in which every song ever recorded was one search away.

item.title: MySpace
item.description: The site that let you paint your own walls -- and the archive that lost the music.

item.title: MSN Messenger
item.description: The after-school network that ran on nudges, emoticons, and whatever song you were playing.

item.title: Google Reader
item.description: The reader that watched the web for its readers, and the summer the inbox went dark.

item.title: Google+
item.description: The social network a search engine made mandatory, and the bug notice that finally closed it.

item.title: GeoCities
item.description: A town of millions of unfinished homepages, and the strangers who stayed up on the last night to carry out the furniture.

item.title: Friendster
item.description: The first social network, which deleted its own memory on the way to becoming a games site.

item.title: eToys
item.description: IPO to Chapter 11 in twenty-two months, a dot-com retail death next to its more famous neighbor.

item.title: Digg
item.description: The front page the crowd voted for, until the crowd voted with its feet.

item.title: del.icio.us
item.description: The site that taught the web to tag, kept alive at the end as a read-only exhibit of itself.

item.title: Cuil
item.description: The search engine that claimed three times Google's index, and could not survive its own launch day.

item.title: AltaVista
item.description: The search engine that was big enough to be the whole web's front door, until the web outgrew the door.

item.title: AOL Instant Messenger
item.description: The buddy list that decided who existed on a given evening, and the December it stopped answering.
